newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: YEAR - CZECH CROWN SEEN HANGING ON C/A DEFICIT.
newsitem.headline: YEAR - CZECH CROWN SEEN HANGING ON C/A DEFICIT.

text.p: The fate of the Czedch crown in 1997 will be tied as never before to the country's ballooning current account deficit which could provoke a downturn in the currency's fortunes late next year, analysts say.

The crown proved remarkably resiliant in 1996, shrugging off a series of domestic political and economic problems to end the year firmly above parity with the mark/dollar basket to which it is pegged each day by the central bank.

Above all, it withstood a near five-fold surge in the current account deficit to more than three billion dollars in the first nine months of the year, supported by a big interest rate differential with western countries.

But analysts said that high interest rates could no longer be taken for granted because of the sagging pace of economic growth, raising the prospect that the crown could find itself exposed to the full force of its current account weakness.
"The risk of the trade deficit is really growing," said Petr Kulka of Girocredit Banka in Prague.

"What I fear is that if they are going to cut interest rates the Czech crown will really go out of range. What they could do is devalue and cut the interest rates at the same time, and that can happen," he added.

The crown is fixed daily against the mid-point of a mark/dollar basket made up of two-thirds marks and one-third dollars. The Czech currency can be fixed up to 7.5 percent above or below the mid-point of the basket.
In recent months it has remained around 2.5 to three percent above the mid- point, or around 27.5 crowns to the dollar and 17.5 crowns to the mark.

The Czech National Bank (CNB) tightened monetary policy in a two-pronged attack in the summer in order to combat inflation which has stubbornly stuck at between 8.5 percent and nine percent throughout the year.

At the end of June the CNB raised its key discount rate one full percentage point to 10.5 percent and then raised minimum reserve requirements for commercial banks to 11.5 percent from 8.5 percent on August 1.
The result has been a dramatic decline in M2 money growth to 9.8 percent year- on-year in October compared with 22.4 percent in the same month in 1995.
However, growth in gross domestic product (GDP) has also declined precipitously to just 3.6 percent in the third quarter from 6.3 percent in same period last year.
The direction that official interest rate policy takes, therefore, will depend on the relative importance attached to increasing growth or, alternatively, reducing inflation.

Analysts said that the most likely resolution to the conundrum was a wait and see policy from the central bank until the middle of the year followed by a cut in interest rates if inflation shows signs of coming down.

"The decrease in M2 growth is positive...but I think that the central bank will wait (before cutting interest rates) until these positive M2 figures translate into a visible decrease in inflation," said Martin Kupka of Patria Finance.
All of the analysts polled by Reuters said the second half of the year would be crucial.
Tomas Becvar, a dealer at Komercni Banka, expected the crown to strengthen slightly during the first quarter before attention refocuses on the trade deficit bringing the crown back down.
"I think during the first quarter of the year..the Czech crown could appreciate again, then later during the year we expect it slowly to come back to central parity," he said.

"I think the trade deficit still could be a relatively big problem," he added. In mid-December the Czech Parliament passed a balanced 1997 budget based on growth in GDP of 5.4 percent, average annual inflation of 8.6 percent, a current account deficit of 5.8 percent and average unemployment of 3.3 percent.
However, many private analysts take a less sanguine view, especially of the prospects for the current account.
-- Prague Newsroom, 42-2-2423-0003
